name: East Javanese kingdoms (Medang, Kahuripan, Kediri, Singhasari)
summary: Hindu-Buddhist kingdoms of East Java after the court moved east from central Java (929): King Airlangga’s Kahuripan, Kediri with its poetry, and Singhasari, whose fall led to Majapahit (1293).

location.value: East Java, Indonesia, centred on the Brantas River valley (around today’s Kediri, Malang and Surabaya).

terrain.value: Volcanic plains and the Brantas River valley.

climate.value: Tropical monsoon: hot all year, with a wet season (November–April) and a dry season.

resources.value: Rich volcanic soil for wet rice, timber, and ports for the spice trade from the eastern islands.

disasters.value: Merapi eruption may have caused the move east (929).

population.value: Perhaps one to two million in the Brantas valley and coast.

urbanisation.value: Royal capitals such as Kahuripan (near the Brantas estuary), Dahanapura (Daha, near Kediri) and Singhasari; ports such as Tuban and Hujung Galuh.
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Kahuripan; Kediri Kingdom; Singhasari (checked 8 Nov 2026)

migration.value: The court moved from Central Java to East Java under Mpu Sindok (929), perhaps after eruptions or wars.

economicBase.value: Wet-rice farming in the Brantas valley and trade in spices, rice and other goods.

tradeRoutes.value: Sea trade with China, India, Srivijaya and the spice islands of eastern Indonesia.

wealth.value: Rich from rice and trade; Kediri was described in Chinese sources as a wealthy kingdom.

moneyAndTax.value: Gold and silver coins (masa), later Chinese copper coins; taxes in rice and labour.

inequality.value: Kings and nobles, Hindu and Buddhist priests, merchants, farmers and slaves.

governmentType.value: Hindu-Buddhist monarchies: Medang (to 1006), Kahuripan (1019–45), Janggala and Kediri (Panjalu, 1042–1222), then Singhasari (1222–92).
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Kahuripan; Kediri Kingdom; Singhasari (checked 8 Nov 2026)

keyRulers.value: Airlangga of Kahuripan; Jayabhaya of Kediri (1135–59); Ken Arok; Kertanegara of Singhasari (from 1268).
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Kahuripan; Kediri Kingdom; Singhasari (checked 8 Nov 2026)

succession.value: Within royal families, but often violent: Ken Arok took the throne from Kediri (1222); Jayakatwang killed Kertanegara (1292).
succession.source: Wikipedia: Kahuripan; Kediri Kingdom; Singhasari (checked 8 Nov 2026)

institutions.value: The royal court, temple and monastery lands (sima) free of tax, and village heads.

stability.value: A rebellion by the vassal king Wurawari destroyed the capital and killed King Dharmawangsa (1006); Airlangga rebuilt the kingdom (1019) and divided it between his two sons (1045).

eliteConflict.value: Rival heirs and princes; Janggala and Kediri fought, and Kediri overthrew Singhasari (1292).

armyAndTech.value: Infantry with spears and krises, and fleets that sailed to Sumatra and Bali.

majorWars.value: Jayakatwang of Kediri killed King Kertanegara of Singhasari (1292); a Mongol fleet arrived the next year.

territoryChange.value: Singhasari sent the Pamalayu expedition to Sumatra (1275) and took Bali (1284).

alliancesRivals.value: Singhasari’s wealth drew the attention of Kublai Khan of Yuan China; Singhasari allied with Champa.

scienceEducation.value: Old Javanese literature flourished: Mpu Kanwa’s Arjunawiwaha under Airlangga, and Mpu Sedah’s Bharatayuddha in Kediri.
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Kahuripan; Kediri Kingdom; Singhasari (checked 8 Nov 2026)

openness.value: Open to trade and new ideas from abroad.

communicationTransport.value: Boats on the Brantas River and sea ships along the coast; footpaths between villages.

religion.value: Hinduism (mostly Shaiva) and Buddhism, often combined; Kertanegara practised Tantric Buddhism.

languageWriting.value: Old Javanese written in the Kawi script; Sanskrit for some religious texts.

artsArchitecture.value: Temples (candi) such as Kidal, Jago and Singhasari, and fine stone statues such as the Prajnaparamita.

socialStructure.value: King and royal family, priests, nobles and officials, farmers and craftsmen, slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the ruler and lineage, with kings seen as incarnations of gods.

dailyLife.value: Most people grew wet rice in villages; temple festivals and shadow-puppet stories were part of life.

neighbours.value: Srivijaya (Sumatra), Bali, the Sunda kingdoms of West Java, and the spice islands.

ideasReligions.value: A blending of Hinduism and Buddhism (Shiva-Buddha) that later shaped Majapahit.

riseSignals.value: Mpu Sindok moved the court to East Java (929).

peakPeriod.value: Airlangga (1019–45), Kediri under Jayabhaya (1135–59), and Singhasari under Kertanegara (1268–92).
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Kahuripan; Kediri Kingdom; Singhasari (checked 8 Nov 2026)

declineSignals.value: Kertanegara was killed in a revolt from Kediri (1292).

outcome.value: Raden Wijaya used the Mongol army to defeat Kediri and founded Majapahit (1293).

overallCertainty.value: Known from chronicles, inscriptions and archaeology; dates and numbers are approximate.
